title: Banking basics: app, website and branch
description: The original 10 lessons: learn everyday banking with comparisons, matching and step-by-step practice.

lessons.title: What is a current account?
lessons.description: Your everyday account. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Your everyday account

A current account is where your pay goes in and your bills come out.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like a locked drawer behind the counter. Only you have the key.

Your debit card

Your debit card uses money from your account. A payment may first appear as pending before it is fully processed.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like handing over cash, but you don’t have to carry the cash.

Check it any time

You can see your money in the app, on the website, or at a cash machine.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like asking the cashier for your balance, when the service is available.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Match each item to what it does
questions.explanation: 💳 Debit card → Pay in shops; 🗄️ Current account → Holds everyday money; 🏧 Cash machine → Take out cash

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: A debit card takes money from your ___.
questions.explanation: A debit card takes money from your account.

questions.prompt: Which one is like a locked drawer in a branch?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Your current account.

lessons.title: Sort code and account number
lessons.description: Sort code. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Sort code

A sort code has 6 numbers, like 12-34-56. It shows which bank you use.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like the address of the building.

Account number

A NatWest account number has 8 digits. Together with the sort code, it identifies your account.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like the number on your drawer inside.

Getting paid

To get paid, give your name, sort code and account number. Never give your PIN.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like writing your details on a paying-in slip.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Match the numbers
questions.explanation: 6 numbers → Sort code; 8 numbers → Account number; 4 numbers → Card PIN (secret)

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: A sort code has ___ numbers.
questions.explanation: A sort code has 6 numbers.

questions.prompt: What should you NEVER tell anyone?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Your PIN.

lessons.title: Is my money safe?
lessons.description: Banks follow rules. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Banks follow rules

UK banks must follow strict rules. Official bodies check them.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like a branch that gets visits from an inspector.

The FSCS

If a bank fails, a scheme called the FSCS can pay back your savings, up to a limit.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like a safety net for eligible deposits if an authorised bank fails. Check which accounts and firms are covered.

Check the limit

The limit can change. Check it on the FSCS website before you save a lot.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Or ask an adviser at the desk.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: The FSCS protects your ___ up to a limit.
questions.explanation: The FSCS protects your savings up to a limit.

questions.prompt: Match the word to its job
questions.explanation: 🛡️ FSCS → Protects savings; 📜 Regulator → Checks the rules; 📞 Your bank → Where you ask questions

questions.prompt: Where do you check the FSCS limit?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: The FSCS website.

lessons.title: Download and log in
lessons.description: Find the app. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Find the app

Open your phone’s app store and search for NatWest. Choose the one made by NatWest.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like finding the right branch on the high street.

Log in

Enter your details. The app may send a code to your phone.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like showing your ID at the counter.

Make it quick

Set Face ID, a fingerprint or a passcode. Next time you log in faster.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like staff who know your face.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Put these in order
questions.explanation: Open the app store → Search for NatWest → Download the app → Log in

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: Always download apps from your phone’s official ___.
questions.explanation: Always download apps from your phone’s official app store.

questions.prompt: What makes logging in faster?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Face ID or a passcode.

lessons.title: Your home screen
lessons.description: Your balance. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Your balance

Your account shows balances and transactions. Check pending payments and bills still to come before deciding what you can spend.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like asking the cashier for your balance.

Payments list

Under it is a list of money in and money out. Tap one to see more.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like a printed statement.

Alerts

Switch on alerts to get a message when money arrives or leaves.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like a friendly cashier giving you a ring.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Match the item to its meaning
questions.explanation: 💷 Balance → Money you have now; 🧾 Payments list → Money in and out; 🔔 Alerts → Messages about your money

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: Your ___ is shown at the top of the screen.
questions.explanation: Your balance is shown at the top of the screen.

questions.prompt: Money leaving your account is called…
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: A payment.

lessons.title: Pay someone
lessons.description: Add the person. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Add the person

Tap Pay. Add their name, sort code and account number.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like filling in a paying-in slip.

Check carefully

Check every number. A wrong number can send money to the wrong person.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like reading the slip twice before you hand it over.

Confirm

Follow the confirmation steps only when you are sure. Check the payment status afterwards: it may be pending, completed or unsuccessful.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like the cashier stamping your slip.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order
questions.explanation: Tap Pay → Add name, sort code, account number → Check the numbers → Confirm

items: Add name, sort code, account number

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: Always ___ the numbers before you pay.
questions.explanation: Always check the numbers before you pay.

questions.prompt: Match the numbers
questions.explanation: 6 numbers → Sort code; 8 numbers → Account number; £ → Amount to pay

lessons.title: Log in online
lessons.description: Go to the website. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Go to the website

Type natwest.com into your web browser.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like walking up to the right shop front.

Check the address

Start from the official NatWest website and check the address carefully. HTTPS or a padlock means an encrypted connection, not proof that a website is genuine.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like checking the sign above the door.

Extra security

You may get a code by text. This is normal. Only you should use it.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like the cashier asking one more question.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: The address should say ___.com
questions.explanation: The address should say natwest.com

questions.prompt: A code arrives by text when you log in. It is…
options: Something to read to a caller
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Extra security for you.

questions.prompt: Match the word to its meaning
questions.explanation: 🔒 Padlock → Encrypted connection, not proof of a genuine site; 🌐 Browser → Where you open websites; 🔑 Code → Only you use it

items: Encrypted connection, not proof of a genuine site

lessons.title: Statements and settings
reading_cards:
Statements

Open Statements to read or download your monthly statements.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like asking staff for a copy.

Settings

Open Settings to change your phone number or address.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like filling in a change of address form.

Proof of address

Some places accept a statement as proof of address. Ask them first.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like asking the branch for a letter.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Match the item to its job
questions.explanation: 📄 Statement → Record of your money; ⚙️ Settings → Change your details; 🏠 Address → Keep it up to date

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: Keep your phone number and ___ up to date.
questions.explanation: Keep your phone number and address up to date.

questions.prompt: Where do you change your phone number?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Settings.

lessons.title: Spot a scam
lessons.description: Scams are common. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Scams are common

Scammers pretend to be your bank. They call, text or email.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Ask staff through a bank branch or a contact route you found independently; appearances alone do not prove identity.

Never share

Your bank will never ask for your PIN, or ask you to move money to a “safe account”.

In everyday terms / at a branch: A cashier would never ask for your PIN.

Hang up and call back

If unsure, hang up. Use another phone, or make sure the call has ended, then contact your bank using the number on your card.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Or walk into a branch and ask.
checklist: Practise explaining one thing from this lesson in your own words.
Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: A caller says “move your money to a safe account”. You…
options: Hang up and call your bank
questions.explanation: The correct answer is: Hang up and call your bank.

questions.prompt: Fill in the gap: Your bank will never ask for your ___.
questions.explanation: Your bank will never ask for your PIN.

questions.prompt: Match the item to its meaning
questions.explanation: 🚨 Scam → A trick to steal money; 📞 Hang up → Stop the call; 💳 Number on card → Safe number to call

lessons.title: Getting help
lessons.description: Ask in the app. Learn with everyday examples.
reading_cards:
Ask in the app

Use Help in the app to chat or call. No question is silly.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like going to the help desk.

Find a branch

Use the branch finder to see opening times and your nearest branch.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Like asking where the nearest branch is.

Bring someone

You can ask a trusted person to come with you.

In everyday terms / at a branch: Staff are used to helping people who are new.

Write down anything you want to ask your bank. Never enter real account details in this prototype.

questions.prompt: Where can you ask for help?

questions.explanation: The correct answer is: The Help section in the app.

questions.prompt: Match the way to get help
questions.explanation: 💬 Chat → Type your question; 📞 Call → Speak to someone; 📍 Branch → Talk face to face
